items.text: Wake at a consistent time and get up without hitting snooze

items.text: Get bright light within 30 to 60 minutes: open the curtains or step outside

items.text: Drink a large glass of water

items.text: Make your bed
Move your body for 5 to 10 minutes: stretch, walk, or a light workout
Brush your teeth and wash your face, or splash with cold water to wake up
Do 5 minutes of breathing, meditation, or quiet before the noise starts
Write your top 3 priorities for the day

items.text: Eat a protein-forward breakfast

items.text: Take any vitamins or supplements
Delay caffeine until about 90 minutes after waking

items.text: Shower and get dressed
Review your calendar and to-do list for the day
Keep your phone and email out of the first 30 to 60 minutes

items.text: Pick 2 to 3 recipes that reheat well

Check what you already have in the fridge, freezer, and pantry
Write a shopping list grouped by store section

Roast a big tray of mixed vegetables
Make one sauce or dressing to vary the flavor across meals

Cool food fully before sealing the lids

Clean as you go and wash your containers so next week is easy
Workout clothes: a moisture-wicking top and shorts or leggings

Say no to one thing that drains you

items.text: Get a medical check-up before you start, especially if you're new to running or have any health concerns

items.text: Choose a 16 to 20 week training plan that matches your current fitness

items.text: Set a realistic goal: to finish, or a specific target time

items.note: Never try a new gel or drink on race day — test everything in training.

items.text: Prioritize hydration, sleep, and recovery throughout the block

items.note: Resist the urge to cram fitness late — the work is already done.

items.text: Carb-load and hydrate well over the final few days

items.note: Going out too fast is the classic first-marathon mistake.

items.text: After the race: keep moving to cool down, refuel, hydrate, and rest before running again
items.note: Give yourself at least a week of easy recovery before hard training resumes.

items.text: Set today's focus — full body, or a specific split like push, pull, or legs

items.text: Warm up for 5 to 10 minutes with light cardio to raise your heart rate

items.text: Start with the biggest compound lifts while you're fresh — squats, deadlifts, bench, or rows

items.text: Work your upper body with a push and a pull movement
Work your lower body with a squat or hinge and a single-leg movement
Finish the main work with focused core exercises
Use a weight you can control with good form for every rep

items.text: Rest 60 to 120 seconds between heavy sets, less for lighter accessory work
Track each exercise, weight, and reps as you go

items.text: Sip water throughout the session, not just at the end

Stretch the muscles you trained while they're still warm
Log the session and note how it felt for next time

items.text: Dress in moisture-wicking layers you can shed, not cotton
Lace up proper running shoes with tread and life left in them

Cool down with a few minutes of easy walking at the end
Do your static stretches while your muscles are still warm
Log your distance, time, and how you felt

items.text: Close with a moment of stillness and a slow return to your day

items.text: Add load with resistance bands or filled water bottles if you have them

items.text: Keep good form over speed, and stop any move that causes sharp pain

Cool down with 3 to 5 minutes of easy movement to lower your heart rate
Stretch the major muscle groups you worked while they're still warm
Track your exercises, rounds, and reps

items.note: Signal varies by carrier and drops away from windows — test where you'll actually use your phone.

items.text: Look under the kitchen sink and around bins for droppings, traps, or roach signs
Check the front-door lock, buzzer or intercom, and how secure the building entrance feels
Ask exactly what the rent includes — water, heating, electricity, internet, parking
items.note: Utilities and parking can add a lot; get the split in writing before you compare places.

items.text: Note which way the windows face and how much natural light each room gets
Take photos or a short video of the whole place as you walk through
items.note: It makes comparing several viewings easier and starts your move-in condition record.

items.text: Check the roof for missing, curling, or patched shingles and note its rough age
items.note: A roof near the end of its life is one of the biggest single costs you can inherit — ask when it was last replaced.

items.text: Check the gutters and downspouts for sagging, leaks, and where they drain
items.note: Water pooling against the house is behind many foundation and basement problems.

items.text: Walk the foundation and exterior walls, looking for cracks, bulging, or crumbling
items.note: Hairline cracks are normal; wide, horizontal, or stair-step cracks deserve a specialist's look.

items.text: Run the taps, showers, and flush the toilets in every bathroom, watching pressure and drainage
items.note: Slow drains, running toilets, and stains under sinks all hint at plumbing you'll pay for.

items.text: Open the electrical panel and check for labelled breakers, scorch marks, and enough capacity
items.note: Old fuse boxes, aluminium wiring, and no ground can be expensive and a safety issue.

items.text: Test the heating and cooling, and ask when the HVAC was last serviced and the filter changed
Look for pest signs — droppings, gnaw marks, mud tubes, sawdust — in the attic, basement, and corners
items.note: Mud tubes on a foundation wall are a classic sign of termites.

items.text: Check the attic insulation depth and look for daylight, stains, or mould under the roof
Inspect the basement or crawl space for damp, efflorescence, and a musty smell
items.note: A dehumidifier running hard or fresh paint on the lower walls can be hiding a moisture problem.

items.text: Open and close the garage door and test its auto-reverse safety
Check that windows and doors open, close, and lock, and look for fogging between double-glazed panes
Look under sinks and around the water heater for leaks, corrosion, and its age
items.note: Most water heaters last 8-12 years; note the manufacture date on the label.

items.text: Test a sample of outlets and switches, plus the GFCI outlets in kitchens and bathrooms
Walk the boundaries and compare fences and structures against the property lines
items.note: Fences and sheds don't always sit on the legal boundary — the survey is what counts.

items.text: Check for even floors and doors that latch; a door that won't close can signal settling
Hire a licensed inspector for anything structural, electrical, or you can't safely reach
items.note: This checklist helps you spot issues and ask better questions — it doesn't replace a professional inspection.

items.text: Read the whole lease, including the small print and any addendums, before signing anything
items.note: Verbal promises don't count — if it isn't written in the lease, assume it won't happen.

items.text: Confirm the rent amount, due date, accepted payment methods, and any late fees
Check the deposit amount, what it covers, and the exact conditions for getting it back
items.note: Ask how and when it's returned, and what counts as normal wear versus a deduction.

items.text: Confirm the lease start and end dates, and whether it renews automatically or goes month-to-month
Read the early-termination clause and what breaking the lease actually costs
items.note: Know the notice period and penalty before you sign — plans change.

items.text: Check who pays which utilities and services — water, heat, electricity, gas, internet, trash
items.note: Get the split in writing; 'utilities included' sometimes comes with a cap.

items.text: Review the pet policy, any pet deposit or rent, and the rules on guests and subletting
Note exactly which repairs and maintenance are yours versus the landlord's
items.note: Clarify who handles a blocked drain, a broken appliance, or a heating failure, and how fast.

items.text: Confirm parking, storage, and any shared-space details in writing
Check the rules on rent increases and how much notice you'll get
Understand the landlord's right of entry and how much notice they must give before visiting
items.note: Most places require reasonable written notice except in an emergency.

items.text: Photograph and video every room before move-in, including existing damage, and share it with the landlord
items.note: Timestamped photos are your best protection against losing the deposit over pre-existing wear.

items.text: Make sure every blank in the lease is filled in, and both parties sign and date it
items.note: Never sign a lease with empty blanks someone could fill in later.

items.text: Save the landlord or property manager's name, phone, email, and address for notices
Keep a signed copy of the lease and every receipt and message in one place
Check your credit and pay down what you can before applying
items.note: A better score can mean a lower mortgage rate — worth doing a few months ahead.

items.text: Set a realistic budget that includes the down payment and monthly costs, not just the price
items.note: Factor in taxes, insurance, maintenance, and any HOA or strata fees — not only the mortgage payment.

items.text: Get a mortgage pre-approval so you know your true price range and can move fast
items.note: Pre-approval is stronger than pre-qualification and shows sellers you're serious.

items.text: Research neighbourhoods, commute, schools, and how the area feels at different times
Make a must-have versus nice-to-have list to keep viewings focused
Line up and attend viewings, and compare each place against your list
items.note: Photograph every place — after a few viewings they blur together.

items.text: Make an offer and negotiate the price and terms with your agent
Hire a licensed home inspector once your offer is accepted
items.note: The inspection can uncover issues worth renegotiating or walking away over — don't skip it to save money.

items.text: Review the property title, survey, and history for liens, disputes, or easements
items.note: A title search makes sure the seller can actually sell and there are no surprise claims.

items.text: Get the property appraised, which your lender will usually require
Compare home insurance quotes and lock in a policy before closing
Budget for closing costs on top of the down payment
items.note: Closing costs often run a few percent of the price — legal fees, taxes, and lender charges add up.

items.text: Do a final walk-through to confirm the condition and that agreed repairs are done
items.note: This is your last chance to catch a new problem before the keys change hands.

items.text: Review and sign the closing documents, and keep copies of everything
Set up utilities, change your address, and collect the keys and any codes or manuals
Take everything out and sort it into keep, repair, and let go
items.note: If you haven't worn it in a year and it isn't sentimental or seasonal, it's probably a let-go.

items.text: Try on the keep pile and check fit, wear, and whether you actually reach for it
Note the real gaps: what you own but can't complete an outfit with
items.note: Gaps are more useful than trends — a missing pair of everyday shoes beats another statement piece.

items.text: Pick a small colour palette so new pieces mix with what you already own
items.note: A few neutrals plus one or two accent colours multiplies the outfits you can make.

items.text: List the basics worth replacing — worn-out staples do more work than trend pieces
Set a budget and decide where it's worth spending more versus saving
items.note: Spend on the things you wear most and that take a beating — shoes, outerwear, everyday denim.

items.text: Check the weather you actually dress for, not just the calendar season
Read care labels before buying — dry-clean-only adds hidden cost and effort
items.note: 'Hand wash' or 'dry clean only' on a basic you'll wear weekly often isn't worth it.

items.text: Feel the fabric and check the seams, buttons, and stitching for quality
Favour versatile pieces that work across several outfits and occasions
Try things on rather than guessing your size across brands
items.note: Sizing varies wildly between brands — the number on the label means little.

items.text: Compare prices across stores and check for end-of-season sales before buying
Keep receipts and tags until you're sure, and note the return windows
items.note: Online returns especially have deadlines — don't let the window close on something that didn't work.

items.text: Donate, sell, or recycle what you're letting go rather than letting it pile up
items.note: Clearing out makes space and shows you what you actually own and wear.

items.text: Store off-season clothes clean and protected to make room and keep them fresh
items.note: Wash before storing — body oils and stains set over months and attract moths.

items.text: Write down what you actually need the device to do before you shop
items.note: Buying for your real use, not the spec sheet, saves you from paying for power you'll never touch.

items.text: Set a budget range, and decide whether last year's model at a discount does the job
items.note: The newest model is often a small upgrade for a big price jump — compare it against the previous generation.

items.text: Shortlist a few models and compare the specs that actually matter for your use
Read recent user reviews, not just the star rating, for real-world problems
items.note: Sort reviews by most recent and most critical — that's where deal-breakers and reliability issues show up.

items.text: Search the model name plus 'problems' or 'recall' to check for common faults
Confirm it's compatible with what you already own — cables, ports, ecosystem, software
items.note: Check ports, wireless standards, and whether it plays nicely with your phone, OS, or smart-home setup.

items.text: Compare prices across several retailers, including refurbished and open-box
items.note: Manufacturer-refurbished gear is often much cheaper with the same warranty.

items.text: Check whether a sale is coming up before you buy at full price
items.note: Big shopping events and new-model launches routinely drop prices — a short wait can save a lot.

items.text: Read the return policy and return window before buying, especially online
items.note: Know how long you have and who pays return shipping if it isn't right.

items.text: Check the warranty length and what it actually covers
See which accessories are included and which you'll need to buy separately
items.note: A cheap deal can cost more once you add the case, cable, or storage it doesn't come with.

items.text: Factor in running costs — subscriptions, batteries, ink, storage, or energy use
Buy from a reputable seller to avoid counterfeits and warranty problems
items.note: On marketplaces, check the seller is the brand or an authorised dealer — grey-market gear can void the warranty.

items.text: Keep the receipt, warranty, and box until you're sure it works and you're keeping it
items.note: You'll need the receipt for warranty claims and returns — save a photo of it too.

items.text: Register the product and install any updates or security before daily use
List everyone you're buying for so no one gets forgotten at the last minute
Set a total budget and a rough amount per person
items.note: A per-person number keeps the total from creeping up gift by gift.

items.text: Jot down each person's interests, hobbies, sizes, and anything they've hinted at
items.note: The best gifts come from paying attention all year — keep a running note on your phone.

items.text: Check for wish lists or registries before guessing
items.note: A wish list takes the pressure off and cuts down on returns and duplicates.

items.text: Note sizes and any allergies or preferences for clothing, food, or beauty gifts
Brainstorm a few ideas per person across a range of prices
Consider experiences or consumables for people who already have plenty of stuff
items.note: A class, a meal, or a subscription is often more welcome than another object to store.

items.text: Consider a handmade or personalised gift where it fits — they carry more meaning
Track what you've bought, for whom, and where, in one running list
items.note: One list stops you double-buying and shows at a glance who still needs a gift.

items.text: Order early to beat shipping deadlines and stock running out
items.note: Popular items sell out and shipping slows near holidays — early is cheaper and less stressful.

items.text: Check delivery dates and any customs or shipping fees for gifts sent abroad
Buy wrapping paper, gift bags, tape, and cards in one trip
items.note: Grab a little extra — you always need one more roll of tape or a spare gift bag.

items.text: Ask for gift receipts and keep them somewhere you'll find them
items.note: A gift receipt lets the recipient exchange or return without seeing the price.

items.text: Set aside time to wrap rather than leaving it all to the last night
Keep a couple of small spare gifts on hand for anyone you missed
items.note: A few generic backups save you when an unexpected gift arrives or you forgot someone.

items.text: Write down your main reason for the visit and what you hope to resolve
items.note: Leading with your top concern means it gets covered even if the visit runs short.

items.text: List your current symptoms — when each started, how often, and what makes it better or worse
Bring an up-to-date list of your medications and doses, including supplements
items.note: Over-the-counter meds and vitamins count; a clear photo of each label works too.

items.text: Note any allergies and past reactions to medications
Write your questions in priority order
items.note: You'll get to the ones that matter even if time runs out.

items.text: Pack your insurance card and a photo ID
Gather recent test results, scans, or reports from other clinics
items.note: Request copies ahead of time if another office is holding them.

items.text: Note relevant family medical history, such as heart disease, diabetes, or cancer
Bring home-tracked numbers if you monitor them — blood pressure, blood sugar, or weight
List other doctors or specialists you see, and what they treat
Confirm the date, time, location, and any prep like fasting or forms
items.note: Some blood tests require skipping food that morning — check when you book.

items.text: Have a way to take notes during the visit — a small notepad or your phone
Arrange for someone to come along if you'd like a second set of ears
Know which pharmacy you use so any new prescription can be sent there
List every medication you take, with its brand and generic name
items.note: Include prescriptions, over-the-counter meds, vitamins, and supplements.

items.text: Record the dose and exactly when you take each one
Note what each medication is for
items.note: It's easier to spot a duplicate or an error when you know the purpose.

items.text: Set daily reminders for each dose time
items.note: A phone alarm or a weekly pill organizer both cut down on missed doses.

items.text: Track refill dates and reorder a few days early
items.note: Ordering before you hit the last pill avoids a gap over weekends or holidays.

items.text: Write down any side effects and when they started, to share with your doctor
Ask your pharmacist to check for interactions whenever a new medication is added
Keep your pharmacy's name, phone number, and hours saved
Store medications as directed — cool, dry, and out of reach of children
items.note: A few need refrigeration; check the label or ask the pharmacist.

items.text: Note any special instructions, like taking with food or avoiding certain drinks
Keep a copy of the list in your wallet or phone for emergencies
Bring the current list to every appointment and update it after changes
Safely dispose of expired or discontinued medications
items.note: Many pharmacies have take-back bins; avoid flushing unless the label says to.

items.text: Review the whole list with your doctor at least once a year
Confirm the date, time, and location, and add it to your calendar
Bring your insurance or dental plan card and a photo ID
items.note: Check what your plan covers so there are no surprises at checkout.

items.text: Brush and floss before you go
Write down any concerns — a sensitive tooth, bleeding gums, jaw pain, or a chip
items.note: Note when it started and what triggers it, like cold or chewing.

items.text: List your current medications and any recent changes
items.note: Some medications affect bleeding or cause dry mouth, which the dentist should know.

items.text: Update your medical history form, including allergies
Prepare questions about brushing, flossing, whitening, or a treatment you're weighing
Arrange a ride ahead of time if you're having sedation or a procedure
Bring any prior X-rays or records if you're seeing a new dentist
Arrive about 15 minutes early to fill out forms
Ask about anything flagged during the exam and what your options are
Confirm the cost and what your insurance covers before agreeing to treatment
Book your next cleaning before you leave
items.note: Most people are due for a check-up every six months.

items.text: Schedule any follow-up treatment and note the aftercare instructions
items.note: Write down aftercare while it's fresh — what to eat, when to resume brushing the area.

items.text: Confirm your guest count and check for allergies or dietary needs
items.note: Vegetarian, gluten-free, or nut allergies shape the whole menu — ask when you invite.

items.text: Pick a loose theme or cuisine to tie the courses together
Plan an appetizer or two that can be served cold or at room temperature
items.note: Something you make ahead frees you up while guests arrive.

items.text: Choose a main course you're comfortable cooking, plus two sides
Balance the menu so not everything needs the oven or stove at once
items.note: One oven dish, one stovetop, and one cold dish is easy to manage solo.

items.text: Select a dessert you can make the day before
Plan drinks — wine or a signature cocktail, plus a non-alcoholic option
Write a full shopping list grouped by store section, and note what you already have
Shop for non-perishables and drinks a few days ahead; buy fresh items the day before
Prep what you can in advance — chop, marinate, make sauces, and set out serving dishes
items.note: Label make-ahead components in the fridge so nothing gets forgotten.

items.text: Write a cooking timeline that counts backward from serving time
items.note: Note what goes in the oven when, and what can rest while you plate.

items.text: Set the table and arrange serving spoons and platters earlier in the day
Have a simple backup ready in case a dish doesn't work out
items.note: A good cheese board or a pasta you can throw together saves the night.

items.text: Plan seating, music, and a tidy space for coats and bags
Pick your recipes and read each one all the way through before starting
items.note: Reading ahead catches a two-hour chill or a step you'd otherwise discover too late.

items.text: Check you have every ingredient in the right amount, and note any substitutions
items.note: Baking is less forgiving than cooking — swapping baking soda for powder won't work.

items.text: Take butter, eggs, and dairy out early if the recipe wants them at room temperature
items.note: Room-temp ingredients cream and emulsify far better than cold ones.

items.text: Gather all tools — bowls, whisk, mixer, pans, parchment, and a scale
Grease and line your pans before you start mixing
Measure ingredients precisely, ideally by weight with a kitchen scale
items.note: Weighing flour avoids the packed-cup error that makes bakes dry and dense.

items.text: Preheat the oven and check it with an oven thermometer
items.note: Many home ovens run 10-15°C off, which is enough to ruin a delicate bake.

items.text: Follow the mixing method exactly — creaming, folding, and order all matter
Set a timer for each batch and check a few minutes before it's due
Test for doneness with a skewer, a gentle press, or the internal temperature
Cool bakes on a wire rack so the bottoms don't turn soggy
items.note: Frost or glaze only once fully cool, or it will melt and slide off.

items.text: Decorate, glaze, or dust once everything has cooled
Store each item the right way once cool
items.note: Airtight at room temperature for most; the fridge or freezer for cream-based bakes.

items.text: Clean as you go and wash tools between mixing wet and dry ingredients
Stock cooking fats — a neutral oil, olive oil, and butter
items.note: A neutral oil for high heat and olive oil for finishing covers most cooking.

items.text: Keep vinegars and acids on hand, like white, balsamic, and a lemon or two
items.note: A splash of acid brightens almost any dish that tastes flat.

items.text: Restock everyday spices and dried herbs, and toss any that have lost their smell
items.note: Ground spices fade after about a year — if it barely smells, it won't season.

items.text: Keep baking basics — flour, sugar, baking soda, baking powder, and salt
Stock pantry carbs like rice, pasta, and a few tins of beans or lentils
Keep flavor builders — garlic, onions, stock cubes, soy sauce, and tomato paste
Restock dairy and eggs, plus a long-life milk or alternative as backup
Buy fresh fruits and vegetables you'll actually use this week
items.note: Buying only what you'll cook cuts the produce that rots in the drawer.

items.text: Check expiration and best-before dates and rotate older items to the front
items.note: Front-to-back rotation is how shops keep stock from expiring unnoticed.

items.text: Restock kitchen paper, foil, parchment, cling film, and storage bags
Check dish soap, sponges, and surface cleaner
Replace worn-out tools — a dull knife, a scratched pan, or a cracked spatula
items.note: A sharp knife is safer than a dull one, which slips instead of cutting.

items.text: Make sure you have the basics — a chef's knife, cutting board, and a few good pans
Organize shelves and containers so you can see what you have
items.note: Clear jars and a quick inventory stop you rebuying what's already there.

items.text: Gather your bank, card, and cash records for the month
Note your total income for the month
List and categorize every expense — housing, food, transport, and the rest
items.note: Grouping spending is what turns a pile of transactions into a picture.

items.text: Compare what you spent against what you planned, category by category
Flag the categories that went over and note why
items.note: The 'why' tells you whether it was a one-off or a habit forming.

items.text: Review recurring subscriptions and memberships, and cancel what you no longer use
items.note: Small monthly charges are the easiest spending to forget and the easiest to cut.

items.text: Scan for any fees, unfamiliar charges, or double bills
Check upcoming large or irregular expenses and set money aside now
items.note: Insurance, tuition, and annual renewals hurt less when you save for them monthly.

items.text: Note how much you saved this month and compare it to your goal
Set a savings target for the coming month
Review your debt balances and the payments due
Update your budget or tracking spreadsheet with this month's numbers
Confirm or set up an automatic transfer to savings on payday
items.note: Automating savings means it happens before you can spend it.

items.text: Review your progress toward longer-term financial goals
Pick one thing to change next month and write it down
items.note: One deliberate tweak a month adds up faster than a total overhaul you abandon.

items.text: Confirm the filing deadline for your region and put it in your calendar
items.note: Deadlines and forms differ by country — check your local tax authority's dates.

items.text: Gather all income statements from employers and any freelance or contract work
Collect records of interest, dividends, and any investment gains or sales
Pull together receipts and records for deductible expenses
items.note: If you're not sure something is deductible, keep it anyway and ask when you file.

items.text: Organize records of charitable donations
Gather mortgage, property tax, and loan interest statements
Collect health insurance and medical expense documents
Assemble records for any home-office or self-employment expenses
items.note: Business and home-office claims need clean records — keep them separate from personal spending.

items.text: Review last year's return to catch anything recurring you might forget
items.note: Last year's return is the best checklist for this year's documents.

items.text: Note any life changes this year — marriage, a new child, a move, a new job — that affect your taxes
List the credits and deductions you may qualify for, to check or discuss
Have your bank details ready for a refund or the account you'll pay from
Decide whether you'll file yourself or with an accountant, and book them early
items.note: Good accountants fill up as the deadline nears — reach out well before.

items.text: Set aside money in case you owe a payment
Keep a complete copy of the return and its supporting documents
items.note: Most tax authorities can ask you to prove a claim for several years afterward.

items.text: Note the date and pull current statements for every investment account
items.note: Reviewing on a set schedule beats reacting to every headline.

items.text: Review performance since your last check, not just the last few days
Compare your current asset mix against your target allocation
items.note: Allocation drift is the quiet way a portfolio gets riskier than you intended.

items.text: Note any holding that has grown well above or fallen well below its target weight
Review the fees and expense ratios you're paying on each holding
items.note: Small percentage fees compound into large sums over years — know what you pay.

items.text: Check that dividends and interest are handled the way you want — reinvested or paid out
Review your retirement contributions and whether you're on track for the year
Confirm you've used any tax-advantaged accounts or annual allowances available to you
Revisit your risk tolerance and time horizon — has anything in your life changed?
items.note: A new job, a home, or a child can change how much risk fits.

items.text: Check that beneficiary and account details are current
Note whether rebalancing is needed to return to your target mix
Confirm your investments still match your original plan and goals
Write down the reasoning behind any change you decide to make
items.note: A short note now explains your past self's thinking at the next review.

items.text: Set a date for your next review
List your short-term goals (under a year) with a target amount and date for each
items.note: A number and a date turn a wish into something you can actually track.

items.text: Set medium- and long-term goals — a home, education, retirement — with rough figures
Check your emergency fund against a few months of essential expenses
items.note: Three to six months of costs is a common target, but any cushion beats none.

items.text: List every debt with its balance, interest rate, and minimum payment
Note your debt-payoff progress since your last review
Decide a monthly savings amount and where each portion goes
Review your insurance coverage — health, life, home, vehicle — for gaps
items.note: The point of insurance is the big, rare event you can't self-fund.

items.text: Plan and price out any major purchases coming up
Note your retirement target and whether contributions are on track
Check your credit report and score, and flag any errors
items.note: You're often entitled to a free report — errors are common and worth disputing.

items.text: Review beneficiaries, a will, or estate documents if you have them
Track your net worth — what you own minus what you owe — to see the trend
items.note: The trend over time matters more than the number on any single day.

items.text: Rank your goals so you know what to fund first when money is tight
Schedule your next review — quarterly works well
